chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Salih ibn Razin from Ibn Ashyam from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him)

Regarding a slave who was permitted to trade: a man gave him one thousand dirhams and said to him, 'Buy a person from it, free him on my behalf, and perform Hajj on my behalf with the remainder.' Then the owner of the thousand dirhams died. The slave went and bought his father, freed him on behalf of the deceased, and gave the remainder to him to perform Hajj on behalf of the deceased, so he performed Hajj for him. This reached the mawali (freemen) of his father, his mawali, and the heirs of the deceased, so they all disputed over the thousand dirhams. The mawali of the manumitter said, 'You bought your father with our money.' The heirs said, 'You bought your father with our money.' The mawali of the slave said, 'You bought your father with our money.'

He said, then Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: 'As for the Hajj, it has passed with what is in it and is not returned. As for the manumitted one, he is returned to slavery for the mawali of his father. Whichever of the two parties establishes proof after this that the slave bought his father from their money, they have his slavery.'

key_terms.عبد مأذون: A slave permitted to conduct trade

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a slave buying his father with entrusted funds and freeing him?
ai.summary: In this ruling from Imam al-Baqir (AS), the legal nuance of an 'abd ma'dhun' (slave authorized to trade) using entrusted funds for specific emancipation and pilgrimage duties is clarified. The Imam establishes that the Hajj remains valid regardless of the dispute, but the father's manumotion is reversible: if the father's mawali prove the funds originated from their share, the father reverts to their slavery, highlighting the Shia jurisprudential principle of tracing the source of funds in conditional emancipation.
